questions.q: Emily's app calls an SMS gateway after each order. Today the gateway is slow. The monitor shows a healthy database and 8% server CPU, but the whole site returns 504. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Low CPU means nobody is doing any work. So what are the workers doing?

options.text: Every worker is stuck waiting for the SMS gateway's reply
options.why: Waiting costs no CPU, but it holds the worker. Once all workers are held, nobody is left to handle any other request.

options.text: The server has run out of RAM
options.why: Out of RAM, processes would be killed, or swapping would make CPU and disk look busy. Here the symptoms are an idle CPU and timeouts.

options.text: The database has no index
options.why: The database is stated to be healthy. A slow query would show up in database CPU or locks.

options.text: nginx is misconfigured
options.why: nginx is working fine: it finds no free worker and correctly returns 504.

questions.q: The code below uses a client configured with timeout: 2. Yet on a timeout the user gets a 500. Why?
questions.hint: Symfony HttpClient responses are lazy. On which line does the real wait happen?

options.text: The timeout exception is thrown in toArray(), which is outside the try
options.why: request() returns immediately; the network wait and the exception happen when the response is read. So the read must be inside the try too.

options.text: TransportExceptionInterface can't catch a timeout
options.why: It can: TimeoutException implements this very interface. The problem is not the exception type but the boundary of the try.

options.text: timeout: 2 is too small and must be raised
options.why: Raising it only keeps the worker stuck longer; the exception would still land outside the try.

options.text: timeout doesn't work on GET requests
options.why: The timeout works the same for every HTTP method.

questions.q: Which of these are examples of a bulkhead?
questions.hint: Which ones split a resource into separate compartments, and which just add resources or attempts?

options.text: A semaphore capping calls to the courier API at 5 at a time
options.why: However slow the courier gets, it can never hold more than 5 workers.

options.text: Separate Messenger transports and workers for payments and reports
options.why: Even if the report line gets long, the payment workers keep working from their own queue.

options.text: Raising pm.max_children from 20 to 200
options.why: This makes the pool bigger, not partitioned. The slow dependency will take all 200, just a little later, and you will run out of memory too.

options.text: A separate PHP-FPM pool for the admin panel
options.why: Then an admin's heavy export can't eat the customers' workers.

options.text: Retrying a failed call 5 times
options.why: Retries don't partition anything. They add load to the slow service and to your own workers.

questions.q: A payment API has a normal response time of p50 = 200 ms and p99 = 900 ms. Which HttpClient max_duration is the most reasonable?
questions.hint: The slowest healthy calls should still get through, but when the API is sick workers shouldn't stay stuck long.

options.text: Around 2 seconds
options.why: Comfortably above p99 (900 ms): nearly all healthy calls get through, and when it is sick the worker is freed after 2 seconds.

options.text: 300 ms
options.why: Plenty of calls take longer than that even when healthy, so you would create failures for nothing.

options.text: 60 seconds
options.why: That is almost the default. When the API is sick each worker would be stuck for a minute and the pool would run dry.

options.text: Better to set no limit, payments are important
options.why: Precisely because it is important, it needs a limit. Without one, a slow payment API can drown the whole site.

questions.q: Every job goes into a single Messenger queue. At month end, 5,000 report jobs pile up and payment confirmation messages run 40 minutes late. What is the right fix?
questions.hint: What happens when urgent jobs and slow jobs wait in the same line?

options.text: Use separate transports and separate workers for payments and reports
options.why: Then the report line can't touch the payment line. This is the bulkhead for queues.

options.text: Reduce the timeout in the report handler
options.why: Reports would fail, but the 5,000 messages would still be standing in front of the payments.

options.text: Double the workers on the same queue
options.why: It helps for a while, but next month with 10,000 reports you get the same problem. The line was never split.

options.text: Stop generating reports
options.why: Reports are legitimate work. Move them to their own compartment rather than dropping them.

questions.q: In which of these places can a missing timeout leave a worker stuck indefinitely or for a very long time?
questions.hint: Anywhere your code waits for a reply from another process or machine.

options.text: Calling an external HTTP API
options.why: The default idle timeout is 60 seconds, and total time has no limit at all.

options.text: Running a database query
options.why: In PostgreSQL statement_timeout defaults to 0: a slow query or lock wait can last as long as it likes.

options.text: Sorting an in-memory array
options.why: Nobody's reply is awaited here. It is CPU work, which is exactly the time max_execution_time counts.

options.text: Reading a cache entry from Redis
options.why: Redis is across the network too. Without limits on connect and read, a slow Redis can jam the whole site.

questions.q: Checkouts arrive at 5 a second and the courier normally replies in 0.2 s. There are 20 workers. Which semaphore limit for the courier makes the most sense?
questions.hint: Calls in flight = calls per second × reply time. Leave room for bursts, but not for the whole pool.

options.text: 1: that is exactly the average need, so nothing is wasted
options.why: There is no headroom. Any small burst of checkouts is turned away even though the courier is healthy.

options.text: 5: about 1 is needed on average, with plenty of room, and 15 workers stay free
options.why: 5 × 0.2 = 1 call in flight, so 5 slots absorbs bursts. If the courier slows down, it can hold at most 5 workers.

options.text: 20: every worker may call the courier
options.why: That is the same as having no bulkhead. A slow courier can still take every worker.

options.text: 0: never call the courier and always use the default charge
options.why: This drops the feature completely. The bulkhead should limit the damage, not remove the feature while the courier is healthy.

questions.q: Ryan's API handles 50 requests a second, but on sale day 60 a second arrive. He set no limit. What will you see after 10 minutes?
questions.hint: Ten more arrive every second than leave. Where are they going?

options.text: About 6,000 requests in line, a wait of about 2 minutes, and most replies arriving after the user has left
options.why: 10 × 600 = 6,000 piled up. ÷ 50 = 120 seconds. By then clients have timed out, so the server's effort is wasted.

options.text: The server will slowly catch up, because the crowd will eventually thin out
options.why: The line keeps growing until the crowd thins, and it takes a long time to drain afterwards. Meanwhile users refresh and add even more load.

options.text: Every request will be slightly slower, by about a second, but will succeed
options.why: The delay doesn't stay small, it keeps growing. The wait of the last person in line gets longer every second.

options.text: Only the 10 extra requests will fail, and the other 50 will be fine
options.why: With no limit, nobody is marked as "extra". The line makes everyone slower and in the end everyone suffers.

questions.q: In which situation is 429 right, and in which is 503?
questions.hint: Whose problem is it: one client's, or the whole server's?

options.text: 429 when one API key asks for more than 100 a minute
options.why: 429 is for a client going over its own limit. It is fixed when that client slows down.

options.text: 503 for any low-priority request when the server is full during a sale crowd
options.why: 503 means the server can't cope right now and nobody in particular is to blame. With Retry-After, the client knows when to return.

options.text: 429 for everyone when the server is full
options.why: With 429 a client thinks it asked for too much, but the cause is the overall crowd. A wrong signal triggers wrong behavior.

options.text: When full, return 200 with empty JSON
options.why: 200 means success. An empty reply misleads the client and takes away its chance to retry.

questions.q: What does the listener below return when the limit is exceeded, and where is the mistake?
questions.hint: What is the status code telling the client? And where does it say when the client should return?

options.text: 500 is wrong, it should be 503; and there is no Retry-After header
options.why: 500 means a bug on the server. This is deliberate shedding, so use 503. Without Retry-After, clients will guess and come back too often.

options.text: No mistake, 500 is fine
options.why: A 500 triggers alerts and looks like a bug. You need to tell deliberate shedding apart from a bug.

options.text: Using consume() is wrong, it should be reserve()
options.why: consume() takes a token at once if there is one and fails without waiting if not. That is exactly what shedding needs.

options.text: `create('global')` is wrong, it should use a per-user key
options.why: The goal here is to protect overall capacity, so one key for everyone. A per-user key is a separate per-user rate limit.

questions.q: During a crowd on a site, which request should be shed last of all?
questions.hint: Which is more tied to the business's revenue and the user's trust?

options.text: The request that confirms a payment
options.why: The user has paid or is about to. Shedding it loses revenue and creates messy uncertain payments.

options.text: Exporting the monthly sales report
options.why: Nobody is harmed if it happens later. That is why it is first on the shedding list.

options.text: The "recommended for you" part of search
options.why: The site works without recommendations. It is second on the shedding list.

options.text: The live "how many people are viewing now" counter
options.why: A counter is decoration, not essential. It is the easiest thing to shed.

questions.q: The reports queue has a limit of 500. The worker finishes 100 a minute, and nobody will tolerate waiting more than 10 minutes. Which decisions are right?
questions.hint: limit ÷ speed = wait. And does a limit alone stop stale work?

options.text: With a limit of 500 the longest wait is 5 minutes, within what users tolerate, so the limit can stay
options.why: 500 ÷ 100 = 5 minutes, under 10 minutes. The limit is within tolerance.

options.text: At the limit, return 503 with Retry-After to new requests
options.why: This way the queue stops growing and users know when to come back. That is back-pressure.

options.text: Remove the limit and keep just 1 worker, it will all finish by the end of the day
options.why: With no limit the wait runs into hours, and stale requests get processed too. By then the user no longer wants the answer.

options.text: When the queue is full, delete old messages and insert new ones, without telling anyone
options.why: Silently dropping work amounts to losing data. Turning requests away openly is the polite and safe way.

questions.q: At 3 a.m. Ryan's server is 10% busy, but 80 searches a second arrive and his fixed cap is 50. What happens, and what is the fix?
questions.hint: Does the cap know how busy the server is?

options.text: 30 searches a second are refused for no reason; enforce the cap only while an overload signal says the server is struggling
options.why: A fixed cap has no eyes. Checking load first means a healthy server serves everyone, and the cap still protects it on sale day.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: a cap that refuses requests is exactly what load shedding means
options.why: Shedding is a reaction to overload. Refusing people while the server is idle only loses requests it could have served.

options.text: Raise the cap to 1,000 for good, so nobody is refused
options.why: On sale day a cap of 1,000 no longer protects checkout. You lose the protection you wanted in the first place.

options.text: Switch the response to 429, so the clients know it is their fault
options.why: The status code does not change who is refused. 503 is still right, because the limit is the server's, not one client's.

questions.q: Rachel's app immediately retries every failed gateway call 5 times. Today 60% of gateway calls fail, and 120 clicks arrive per second. The gateway's capacity is 150/second. What happens?
questions.hint: Each failure creates another call. What does the total come to?

options.text: Total calls exceed capacity and the gateway fails even more: a retry storm
options.why: Each click makes on average 1 + 0.6 + 0.36 + ... ≈ 2.4 calls, about 285 in total. That is nearly double capacity, so the gateway can't recover.

options.text: Because of the retries, every click eventually succeeds, so there is no problem
options.why: Retries save some clicks, but the extra calls drown the gateway further. Then the success rate itself drops.

options.text: It will only be slower, but there will be fewer failures
options.why: The failure rate actually rises, because the extra load makes the gateway fail more.

options.text: The gateway is not affected, because retries are only the app's business
options.why: Every retry is a genuinely new call to the gateway. The effect lands directly on the gateway.

questions.q: The breaker has a threshold of 5 and openSeconds of 30. In which situations does a call reach the service?
questions.hint: The states where the breaker is not cut, or where it is time for a test.

options.text: After 3 failures in a row (still CLOSED)
options.why: The threshold is 5, so 3 failures haven't tripped the breaker. Calls still go through normally.

options.text: 10 seconds after the 5th failure
options.why: It is OPEN now and the 30 seconds aren't up. No call goes through, it goes straight to the fallback.

options.text: The first call 31 seconds after the 5th failure
options.why: This is the half-open test. On success the breaker is closed, on failure it opens again for 30 seconds.

options.text: Right after the 5th failure, because the last call is the measure
options.why: The breaker opened on the 5th failure itself. From then on, no call goes through for 30 seconds.

questions.q: The breaker in the code below has a problem. Which one?
questions.hint: What changes on each failure? Where is the threshold?

options.text: It goes OPEN for 30 seconds on the very first failure, and never checks a threshold
options.why: until is always set to time()+30. One small hiccup shuts the service off for 30 seconds: the breaker is far too sensitive.

options.text: Resetting fails to zero on success is wrong
options.why: Resetting on success is right, because we are counting consecutive failures.

options.text: Using the fallback is wrong, it should throw an exception
options.why: Returning an alternative answer on failure is part of what a breaker is for.

options.text: You can't keep the state in a cache
options.why: A cache is the simple, effective place for it, especially Redis, where all servers see the same state.

questions.q: In which cases is retrying reasonable?
questions.hint: Where the next attempt could succeed, and repeating does no harm.

options.text: A GET /payments/{id} call that got a 503
options.why: 503 is temporary, and GET is safe: the result is the same however often you send it.

options.text: POST /charges with an Idempotency-Key, after a timeout
options.why: Because of the key, the gateway recognizes the second call and the money is charged only once.

options.text: Resending the same POST after a 422 Validation Error
options.why: The input itself is wrong, so the same call will always fail. Retrying only adds load.

options.text: POST /charges without a key, after the connection dropped
options.why: If the call already reached the gateway, a second call could charge the money twice. Without a key this is dangerous.

questions.q: On one click, Vue tries 4 times, the Symfony API 4 times and the gateway client 4 times (3 retries each). How many calls can reach the gateway at most, and what is the fix?
questions.hint: The layers multiply, they don't add.

options.text: 64; keep retries in a single layer and add a retry budget
options.why: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. If retries sit in the lowest layer and the others try once, calls fall to 4, and a budget keeps even that in check.

options.text: 12; the fix is to raise the number of retries
options.why: Layers multiply, they don't add. And adding retries only makes the problem worse.

options.text: 64; the fix is to double the retries at every layer
options.why: The number is right, but the fix is backwards: more retries make the product explode even more.

options.text: 4; there is no problem
options.why: That is the count for a single layer. With retries in three layers, it multiplies to 64.

questions.q: Users keep mistyping their district, so the courier API answers 404 again and again. Should those 404s count towards the breaker's threshold?
questions.hint: Is the courier sick, or was our request wrong?

options.text: Yes: any answer other than 200 is a failure
options.why: A 404 here is the courier working correctly and rejecting a bad request. Counting it would trip the breaker on a healthy service.

options.text: No: only network errors and 5xx answers show a sick service
options.why: A 4xx means our request was wrong. Counting only transport errors and 5xx keeps the breaker honest.

options.text: Yes, but only if 5 of them come in a row
options.why: Five typos in a row can still happen on a busy day. The courier would be cut off for everyone although nothing is wrong with it.

options.text: No: nothing should be counted, because only timeouts matter
options.why: Connection errors and 5xx answers also show a sick service. Ignoring them leaves the breaker closed while the service is down.

questions.q: On Nate's site, the product page fetches the price (from the database) and reviews (from an external service) together. The review service fails. Which behavior is right?
questions.hint: Which one can't you buy without, and which one can you?

options.text: Open the page with the reviews part hidden or marked "not available now", price intact
options.why: Reviews are optional and the price is core. With an optional part gone, the customer can still buy.

options.text: Return 500 for the whole page, because the data is incomplete
options.why: That stops sales, though only one piece of decoration was broken.

options.text: Hold the page until the reviews arrive
options.why: The waiting ties up workers, and without a timeout the whole site can slow down.

options.text: Drop the price too: if everything isn't right, show nothing
options.why: That is the opposite of degradation: losing the core part as well.

questions.q: In which of these cases is it safe to serve a stale or default fallback?
questions.hint: Who is harmed by an old or empty answer?

options.text: The "recommended for you" list on a product
options.why: Recommendations a few hours old do no harm, and the page still looks complete.

options.text: Catalog product descriptions, which change once a month
options.why: It is slow-changing data, so an old copy from the cache is almost always right.

options.text: The customer's wallet balance
options.why: A customer who sees a wrong balance may make a wrong decision. "Can't show this right now" is the right answer here.

options.text: Whether a payment succeeded
options.why: Calling an unknown state "success" or "failed" can lose money or charge twice.

questions.q: What is wrong with the code below, for recommendations?
questions.hint: If it fails, who will know? And what kinds of error does it catch?

options.text: Nothing is logged, there is no degraded flag, and \Throwable also hides bugs in your own code
options.why: If recommendations were empty for a month, nobody would know. It needs a log, a degraded flag and a catch for the specific ExceptionInterface.

options.text: Returning an empty list is never right
options.why: For an optional part like recommendations, an empty or stale answer is perfectly right. The problem is the silence.

options.text: Putting the call in a try/catch is wrong, the exception should propagate
options.why: It isn't right to ruin the whole page because an optional part failed.

options.text: There is nothing wrong
options.why: Invisibility is the biggest risk: a failure can go unnoticed for months.

questions.q: A Vue page calls two APIs: product (core) and recommendations (optional). It currently uses `await Promise.all([...])`. What happens when the recommendations API fails, and how do you fix it?
questions.hint: What does Promise.all do on the first failure?

options.text: The whole promise rejects, and the product data is lost too; handle them separately with allSettled
options.why: Promise.all rejects as soon as any one fails. allSettled returns both results separately, so only a failure of the core call is an error.

options.text: Only the recommendations go empty, and the product is fine
options.why: That doesn't happen with Promise.all: on a failure the whole result is discarded.

options.text: Both product and recommendations are retried
options.why: Promise.all does not retry on its own.

options.text: Nothing happens, the browser handles it
options.why: The browser doesn't know which call is core and which is optional. That decision belongs to your code.

questions.q: What should the delivery charge be when the courier fails? Which decisions are right?
questions.hint: Who pays for a mistake, and who gets to find out?

options.text: Use the maximum rate per district, approved in advance
options.why: The business knows and agreed to it, so the company doesn't lose money and the customer can be told it is an "estimate".

options.text: Keep a log and an alert whenever the fallback runs
options.why: Otherwise nobody will know how long the fallback has been running. An alert catches the problem in minutes.

options.text: Quietly return 0 so orders don't get stuck
options.why: Every order then ships with no delivery charge and nobody notices. That is quietly losing money.

options.text: Fall back to the same database that stores the courier rates, which is itself slow right now
options.why: A fallback that leans on the failed dependency will fail too. A fallback has to be independent.

questions.q: Sabir's team renamed a column and ran a rolling deploy. For 5 minutes some users got a 500. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Which versions run side by side during a deploy?

options.text: The old servers were still looking for the column under its old name, which no longer exists in the database
options.why: In a rolling deploy the old code keeps running for a while. If the migration has already run, that code breaks.

options.text: The new code had a bug, so every server failed
options.why: If every server failed, the problem would not have ended in 5 minutes. Here the failures were only on the old servers, and they stop when the deploy completes.

options.text: The database had become slow
options.why: A slow database would give timeouts, not a "column does not exist" error.

options.text: The load balancer was misconfigured
options.why: The load balancer was fine: it was sending traffic to the old servers, which were still running.

questions.q: In which situation is blue/green the most sensible choice?
questions.hint: When does the speed of rollback matter most?

options.text: A big, risky change, where if something goes wrong you must be back within a minute
options.why: The old environment is ready, and flipping the switch takes you back.

options.text: Server capacity is very tight, and no extra servers can be kept
options.why: Blue/green briefly runs two environments, so it needs spare capacity. With limited resources rolling is better.

options.text: You want to test a new feature on 5% of users first
options.why: That is a job for canary: testing on a small slice of traffic first.

options.text: A few small changes every day, at the lowest cost
options.why: For small regular changes, rolling is the simplest and cheapest.

questions.q: In expand-contract, the phone column is being turned into mobile. Which order is right?
questions.hint: The old code must never see a broken state.

options.text: Add mobile, release write-to-both, backfill, read from mobile, and drop phone in a later release
options.why: At every step both old and new code work. The drop comes last, after everyone has moved.

options.text: Rename phone to mobile, then deploy the code
options.why: That breaks the old servers, because they are still looking for phone.

options.text: Drop phone and add mobile, in the same release
options.why: Data is lost, and on rollback the old code can't find phone.

options.text: Deploy the code, then add mobile
options.why: The new code would try to write to a column that doesn't exist yet, which means errors.

questions.q: Which of these are part of a graceful shutdown?
questions.hint: Think of work in progress and new work separately.

options.text: Taking the server off the load balancer before shutdown, so new requests stop coming
options.why: Once no new requests arrive, it is easy to finish the ones in progress.

options.text: A Messenger worker that gets SIGTERM finishes its current message and stops
options.why: This way the message isn't cut off halfway. And if it is, it comes back to the queue.

options.text: Sending SIGKILL straight away, because it is fast
options.why: SIGKILL cuts work in progress off halfway. It is the last resort, not the first.

options.text: Keeping terminationGracePeriodSeconds short so the server goes quickly
options.why: If the time is shorter than the longest request, work in progress gets cut off.

questions.q: A release shipped the new code and "ALTER TABLE user DROP phone" together. Ten minutes later the error rate rose. What would have been the best move, and what now?
questions.hint: Code can be rolled back, but what can't be?

options.text: The mistake was putting the contract in the same release. Now the column has to be restored from backup, and in future the contract goes in a separate release
options.why: After a code rollback, the old code asks for phone but the column is gone. Restoring the data needs a backup. In future, the drop should be a separate, later release.

options.text: Just rolling the code back to the previous version will fix everything
options.why: The old code will ask for the phone column, which no longer exists. It will break too.

options.text: Running the down() migration will bring the data back
options.why: down() only recreates an empty column. The numbers that were in it do not come back.

options.text: Writing a new hotfix and waiting, with no rollback
options.why: A hotfix can take hours, and users get errors meanwhile. You need a rollback plan in advance.

questions.q: Nicole ran the backfill, and only an hour later released the code that writes both columns. Reads then moved to mobile. What do some users see?
questions.hint: Who saved their number between the backfill and the dual-write release?

options.text: Users who signed up in between show no number, because their row was saved to phone only after the copy
options.why: The backfill only copies rows that exist when it runs. Write-to-both must be fully live first, so nothing new slips through.

options.text: Nothing: the backfill keeps watching and copies new rows by itself
options.why: The command copies what exists when it runs, then stops. It does not follow new writes.

options.text: All users lose their number, because mobile starts empty
options.why: The 10,000 existing rows were copied. Only the rows saved after the copy and before dual-write are missing.

options.text: The column cannot be dropped later
options.why: Dropping works as before. The harm is the missing numbers, not the drop.

questions.q: A custom php-fpm Docker image is stopped in a rolling deploy with the default signal, and users report 502s on long requests. What is the likely cause and fix?
questions.hint: What does php-fpm do when it receives SIGTERM?

options.text: php-fpm stops at once on SIGTERM, cutting requests in flight; add STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT to the Dockerfile
options.why: SIGQUIT makes php-fpm finish its current requests first. The terminationGracePeriodSeconds must still be longer than the longest request.

options.text: The readiness probe is too slow; raise periodSeconds
options.why: A slower probe does not change what php-fpm does on the stop signal. Requests in flight are cut by the signal itself.

options.text: Switch to SIGKILL, which stops it more cleanly
options.why: SIGKILL cannot be caught. It kills at once and is the worst choice for in-flight work.

options.text: The Messenger worker is at fault; run messenger:stop-workers
options.why: The 502s come from the web process, not the queue worker.

questions.q: Julia's app is backed up every night at 2 a.m. If the database is destroyed at 1 p.m. on Monday, roughly how much data is lost, and which number is that?
questions.hint: How much time lies between the last backup and the disaster?

options.text: About 11 hours of data: this is the actual data lost in this disaster, to be compared with the RPO
options.why: From 2 a.m. to 1 p.m. is 11 hours. If the RPO target is lower than that, this setup is inadequate.

options.text: Nothing, because a backup exists
options.why: A backup preserves only the state at that moment. Everything written after it is lost.

options.text: Only 1 minute, because everything restores quickly
options.why: Restore speed is about RTO. Lost data depends on how old the backup is.

options.text: The whole day's database
options.why: The backup holds everything up to 2 a.m. Only the 11 hours after that are lost.

questions.q: Which of these help to reduce RTO?
questions.hint: RTO is how long it takes to get running again.

options.text: Keeping a ready app and replica in another region in advance
options.why: After a disaster you then only need to move traffic, not build everything from scratch.

options.text: A written and tested runbook
options.why: People don't guess or hunt around, so time is saved.

options.text: Backing up more often (every hour)
options.why: This lowers RPO (less data lost). It does not make recovery faster.

options.text: Keeping the DNS TTL at 24 hours
options.why: A large TTL can mean traffic takes up to 24 hours to move to the new region, which makes the RTO huge.

questions.q: A small e-commerce startup: users only in the US, a team of 5, and an RTO of 1 hour is acceptable. Which multi-region pattern would you pick?
questions.hint: Match cost and complexity to what is really needed.

options.text: Active-passive: a replica and a ready app in another region
options.why: An RTO of 1 hour is met by active-passive. There are no conflicts, and complexity and cost stay low.

options.text: Active-active, because it is the safest
options.why: It is the most complex and the most expensive. Handling conflicts is an unnecessary burden for a team of 5.

options.text: Nothing, because the cloud provider handles it
options.why: The provider supplies the infrastructure, but the DR plan for your data and app is your responsibility.

options.text: Keep the backup on another server in the same region
options.why: If the whole region goes down, that goes too. Only a separate region protects against a disaster.

questions.q: The runbook below has a problem. Which one?
questions.code:
psql -h replica.region-b -c "SELECT pg_promote();"
# the replica is now primary, point the app at the new host
# bring the old primary back up, it's fine if it recovers
questions.hint: What happens if two primaries can both take writes?

options.text: If the old primary comes back there are two primaries (split brain), so it should be isolated first
options.why: If different writes land in two places, the data can't be reconciled. Keep the old primary stopped or isolated, and bring it back later as a replica.

options.text: pg_promote() should never be used
options.why: It is the right way to turn a replica into a primary.

options.text: Pointing the app at the new host is wrong
options.why: Pointing the app at the new primary is exactly what you should do.

options.text: No problem, the steps are fine
options.why: The last step is dangerous: if the old primary starts on its own, you end up with two versions of the data.

questions.q: A team ran a game day. The target RTO was 30 minutes but it took 90; 40 minutes went on hunting for one secret. Which decisions are right?
questions.hint: What was the purpose of the drill?

options.text: Store the secret in both regions, write it in the runbook, and run the drill again
options.why: The gap has been found, so now fix it and measure again.

options.text: Count the drill a success: we found the problem before a real disaster
options.why: That is exactly what a game day is for. Finding the gap now is far better than finding it on disaster day.

options.text: Change the RTO target to 90 minutes so the drill passes
options.why: The target is set by business need, not by the drill result. Moving the limit just hides the problem.

options.text: Punish the employee responsible for the delay over the secret
options.why: The gap is in the system, not in a person. Punishment makes people hide problems in the next drill.

questions.q: Nicole's invoicing app has a 200 GB database. The business accepts losing about 15 minutes of data and being down about 3 hours, and the budget is tight. Which option fits?
questions.hint: How long does restoring 200 GB take, and what does the RPO need?

options.text: Pilot light: a database replica running in the other region, the app started in a disaster
options.why: Replication keeps the data minutes behind, and starting the app fits within 3 hours. It costs a fraction of a standby region.

options.text: Backup and restore with a nightly backup
options.why: A nightly backup can lose a day of data, and restoring 200 GB at 50 GB an hour takes 4 hours alone. It misses both targets.

options.text: Active-active, because it is the safest
options.why: It would meet the targets, but at the highest cost and complexity. A rung that is cheaper meets them too.

options.text: A second copy of the backup in the same region
options.why: If the region goes down, both copies go. Only a different region protects against a regional disaster.
